chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Thal'abah ibn Maymun, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about the testimony of the blind man, so he said: 'Yes, if it is established/proven.'
ai.seo_question: Is the testimony of a blind person valid in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Baqir (AS) affirms the validity of a blind person's testimony, contingent upon the establishment of their credibility or the specific facts in question. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic principle that physical sensory limitations do not inherently invalidate legal testimony, provided the witness's reliability is verified through other means. It underscores the flexibility of Islamic evidence law in accommodating diverse human conditions.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziyad, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Abu Nasr, from Sa’alba Bin Maymoun, from Muhammad Bin Qays, 
(The narrator) says, ‘I asked Abu Ja’far
<sup>asws</sup> testimony of the blind. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Yes, when it is proved’.
en.sarwar: 1. A number of our people have narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from ibn abu Nasr from Tha‘labah ibn Maymun from Muhammad ibn Qays who has narrated the following: “I once asked abu Ja‘far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam,
about the testimony of a blind man. He (the Imam) said, ‘Yes, it is admissible if he has preserved it.’”
